utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Please, Madam Registrar, kindly call the case scheduled today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-01-48-A, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Halilovic, are you able to follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now ask for the appearances, starting with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. My name is Peter Morrissey, and I appear as counsel for Mr. Halilovic in this matter. With me is co-counsel, Guenael Mettraux. And to assist Mr. Halilovic with interpretation is Mr. Sule Imsirpasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Morrissey. Let me now turn to the representatives of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Peter Kremer, appearing with Laurel Baig and Arthur Buck for the Prosecution, Lourdes Galicia, our case manager, is assisting us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kremer. This afternoon the hearing will be devoted to the submissions by the parties on appeal. The representatives of Mr. Halilovic will have one hour and 30 minutes to finish their submissions in their response. We will then have a 15-minute break. And the OTP will have 45 minutes to develop their submissions in reply. Mr. Halilovic will then be invited to take the floor, if he so wishes, for a short statement of no more than ten minutes. I shall now ask the Defence to continue with their submissions. You may proceed, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, yesterday we were dealing with the Prosecution brief relating to ground one, sub one, and it was section B of that brief, and we had nearly reached the end of that. We were dealing with the inspection team and the relevance that had to the Prosecution case, and we had reached almost to the conclusion of that part and I wish to now conclude that by the following comments. Your Honour, the inspection team role was extensively analysed by the Trial Chamber and whatever lens may be used the evidence remains the same and the focus must always the same. Did that inspection team role of Halilovic give him command authority? The answer to that is no. Did it give him effective control by some other means? And the answer to that is no. I've already pointed to our submissions relating to the behaviour of those alleged subordinates of Halilovic, and I've pointed in particular to the conduct of Zulfikar Alispago. I will briefly mention the conduct of Ramiz Delalic who was another broken link in the chain of command alleged by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber made reference to evidence at paragraphs 508 and 674 to an incident that took place on or about the 10th of September of 1993 at the flat of Zulfikar Alispago. That evidence was significant in that Namik Dzankovic, a member of the inspection team, was present and Delalic displayed disrespect and it would be said aggression concerning his continued participation in any activities in the area. And you can take that into account in considering what respect one gained or any person gained by virtue of their membership of the inspection team. Evidence -- I've referred already to evidence from Witness J and we adopt, generally speaking, the references in our brief and also in our pre-trial -- our Defence final brief in relation to that. As a result the answer to the Defence -- the answer the Defence would pose and the questions or response we make to the Prosecution's answer to the second question concerning the inspection team is to say: No, the acts of Halilovic and the fact that his membership of the inspection team do not indicate effective control. The Trial Chamber's analysis of the power says it doesn't. The evidence considered by the Trial Chamber says that it doesn't. And no one said: Look, I'm from the inspection team, take me seriously. In conclusion, it's not indicative of effective control and in a military setting we adopt, not in precise terms, but the thrust of the question asked by the learned Presiding Judge: What's the effect of the military setting here? If a person's not appointed to command, they're not in command. This is a military organisation, and if they meant to appoint Halilovic to command, there would be an order saying so. Your Honours, I turn now to part C of ground one. In this part the Prosecution assert that, in fact, they did prove effective control by referring to findings and by referring to the evidence. This part, Your Honours, may be regarded as the retrial of the matter by the Prosecution, and we submit in general, as we did at the start, it's oppressive to retry Mr. Halilovic in such a narrow compass as is available on appeal and the difficulties are made manifest by the -- what we describe as the impassioned and skilful closing address delivered yesterday by Mr. Kremer, listing for you evidence on which it is said the Tribunal should have convicted Mr. Halilovic. The argument put by the Prosecution under this heading - and these are some preliminary remarks before we get to the substance of it - do not attempt to revive the argument in the notice of appeal; namely, the de facto command argument. Instead the Prosecution argues in general terms that these are indicators and evidence of effective control. Now, it has the dual effect, as we've submitted before, of constituting an abandonment of the notice or alternatively an inadequate argument of that notice and we've already referred to the waiver arguments. I adopt them again. I won't repeat them in each occasion we say that arises, but we adopt it. However even on its own terms we say it's a meritless ground because the Trial Chamber carefully examined the evidence that's listed under it and because the Prosecution doesn't seek to deal with the exculpatory evidence at all but simply lists it's own evidence and that is appropriate in a closing address at trial, but here their burden is much higher. Your Honours, the Prosecution allege a variety of findings. This section C is divided into three parts, and I propose to deal with them sequentially, different weight to each part. But the Prosecution say first of all that there are findings of the Trial Chamber which indicate a material ability to prevent and those findings are gathered together in argument in the appeal brief of paragraph 2.35. Essentially the Prosecution says Halilovic is found to have had powers pursuant to the inspection team, his inspection team role, powers to resubordinate, powers to issue orders, powers to select accommodation, and, in effect, powers to be inferred from documents that came to and from the alleged IKM which I'll deal with later on. We comment it's doubtful that these can be regarded as findings at all, but what can be said is that the Trial Chamber considered all of these matters in detail in a careful judgement, and we adopt their brief and specifically you'll find assistance at paragraph 97 of the Defence response appeal -- response to this appeal. Your Honours, our answer in detail, however, to these matters is -- and we just cannot deal with it in great detail, but in response to the alleged findings we say that as the Prosecution records -- refers to the issuing of orders by the accused, we remind the Appeals Chamber that the issuing of orders is not a matter that mathematically proves whether a person has effective control. This Tribunal more than most has experience with dealing with the subtleties of orders and whether they do or do not prove effective control in a given situation. It must be shown that the orders given do in fact reflect effective control over the perpetrators. It must be shown that they are relevant to the issues that are before the Court; namely, the effective control by means of a material ability to prevent or punish. For example, a power to bring food to units would not be relevant. Your Honours, I refer just -- there is a great deal of law and on this, it's referred to in our brief but the Blaskic Appeals Chamber at paragraph 69 deals with the type of matters that have to be considered when assessing orders. And in this case the Trial Chamber clearly did do that carefully and step by step, looking at individual orders and looking at their effect as a whole. There was no segmenting by the Trial Chamber but there was a pain-staking approach taken to it. The same considerations apply to the allegations relating to the powers to coordinate the work of the 4th and 6th Corps, powers given under the order establishing the inspection team. The same considerations may be applied to the powers to resubordinate. Now, this matter -- Halilovic evidently did issue orders that were relevant to the resubordination of units and the Trial Chamber dealt with this carefully, and it was open to them to find that notwithstanding issuing these order, that did not give Halilovic effective control. Your Honours, the Prosecution rely in particular to orders relevant to the commander of the 1st Corps, General Karavelic as the subject of some questions from the Bench yesterday, and I propose to deal briefly with a couple of matters raised there. The first order that the Prosecution focused upon was the order Exhibit 161, which was an order dated the 2nd of September of 1993, which was an order by Halilovic to Mr. Karavelic, commander of the 1st Corps, and which instructed him to select 300 soldiers from among a range of units, which included the 9th Brigade. Your Honours, the evidence about that was that Karavelic didn't obey that order by virtue of the authority of Halilovic, but instead approached the commander Delic, and it was pursuant to Delic's instructions that he put into effect a what he was asked to do. It was under the power of Delic, notwithstanding that it was under the hand of Halilovic that particular order that action was taken. And as a result of that, it was well within the Trial Chamber's rights to find as they did. The second Karavelic matter was something that arose yesterday in dramatic form when the Prosecution said that Mr. Karavelic had asked to have the troops returned to him, only to have -- to be told by Halilovic: "You can't have your men back." That allegation seems to be made at page 21, line 13, of yesterday's proceedings. The difficulty with that, Your Honours, is that the Prosecution has been led into overstating the evidence on that point. It's referred to in the brief -- sorry in the trial judgement at paragraphs 304, 306, and 423 and the evidence from the trial appears at Mr. Karavelic's transcript on Wednesday, the 20th of April, at -- just excuse me at paragraph -- at page 75 of that transcript. I'll just take you to it because what's apparent when you examine the evidence is that it is not established that Halilovic refused a request from Karavelic at all. Question at line 15: "Now, what was your response to Mr. Solakovic's request of you to return to Sarajevo?" I just need to pause before I read the answer. We understand this is an appeal hearing, this Tribunal hasn't sat through the evidence and understood everything that lay behind it, but at all events the terms of this are quite clear. "A. I don't recall anything in particular. I don't think I had any specific response. I think that later, I don't know when, whether it was in the same day, in the next day, in a couple of days, I got in touch with Rasim Delic or Sefer Halilovic, I don't remember. It's possible. I cannot confirm that when I requested the return and so on and so forth. I have some idea that perhaps I received some information from somewhere that everything was all right. Nothing else. What else could I do?" You can analyse that any way that you choose, but it could not be constructed into a refusal to Karavelic by Halilovic that he send the troops back. And in fairness to the Prosecution here, Your Honours asked a question at paragraph -- at page 29 yesterday and Mr. Kremer was asked -- was put on the spot effectively without the transcript in front of him of course, and that's a difficult position for everyone, and he did say to the Court I think that that's the cases. Of course what we say is that there isn't any such evidence of Halilovic refusing a request by Karavelic. All there was, in fact, in terms of evidence and -- on this point was that a junior officer named Okovic said that he had hearsay evidence to give about something he was told by Mr. Solakovic that Solakovic had requested to be sent back and that that request had not been accepted, and it wasn't clear who it had not been accepted by; although, Halilovic was at the meeting where it was not accepted. But you couldn't construct that, even that hearsay distant evidence, into a refusal by Halilovic. I would ask you to set aside, therefore, as an incident of Halilovic's effective control over these troops that he refused them to be sent back to Sarajevo at that time. But even if he had have refused, even if the Prosecution had proved those facts, it would not have availed because those troops were in -- in Sarajevo -- in Herzegovina pursuant to an order of -- effectively an order of Delic, although it was under the hand of Halilovic. Your Honours, we've plunged deep into the detail of the trial in doing that and it creates difficulties because at this level it's appropriate to deal on a more general level, and I'm going to try to do that throughout the rest of the submissions. At all events what's submitted is that those findings alleged by the Prosecution simply do not establish what they set out to do, what they claim to do. The Trial Chamber has considered all the evidence and that doesn't avail. The next allegations made by the Prosecution at paragraphs 2.36 to 2.38 is that the findings of the Trial Chamber prove a material ability to punish or to investigate the crimes. We've responded to that at page -- paragraph 98 of the respondent's brief. We apologise that there's a typographical error there which might have caused some confusion in the first couple of lines. It's said that, we refer to "a failure to prevent," whereas we're obviously referring to a failure to punish in that paragraph, but we do apologise for any confusion that that may have caused. The substance of the paragraph makes it clear what we were dealing with. By way of preliminary points there, we would point out that when dealing with evidence about failure to punish, it is not appropriate to deal with a failure to investigate as if that is a separate element. A failure to investigate is really an aspect of a failure to punish and evidence of a failure to investigate may well be evidence relevant to establishing a failure to punish and indeed it may suffice in a certain case. But it is not a separate element. Your Honours, for that reason we submit it's -- it's not appropriate, either on appeal or at any time, to refer to material abilities to perform mere acts. In other words, the reference to material ability is a reference to the material ability to punish, not the material ability to attend a scene or the material ability to make a telephone call. Although it's not grammatically wrong to use the term "material ability" in that way, it's apt to confuse and apt to dilute the meaning of the concept "material ability." It's more appropriate to talk of matters in evidence which support the allegation of material ability to punish. So it might be said in a given case that a person had the ability to issue an order or the ability to attend at a place. In any event, that's a matter of nomenclature and we make the point here because the Prosecution has seen fit to plead a number of functional matters that they allege as constituting material abilities, and we'd ask you that those acts do not take on some legal significance merely by given title of a material ability. They have to be assisting in the normal way as evidence either raising a reasonable doubt or proving the Prosecution case to the required standard. The third preliminary point we make is that there could be in that situation an endless list of potential steps that an individual could be said to have available to them physically, morally, but these are not relevant material abilities. They are simply pieces of evidence. And I take as an example of that the recommend -- the requirement imposed yesterday in the closing speech by -- in submissions by Mr. Kremer of the endless cascade of recommendations that Halilovic could have made. Now, that didn't need to stop where it stopped. The Prosecution could have multiplied those recommendations endlessly. And it's impossible for the Defence to meet that other than to deal in substance with it, with the law itself and with the matters that are raised under it. Your Honour, under this ground we say that apart from those objections and turning to the merits of it, they use a meritless argument all together. The Prosecution argument here rests on effectively the fact that Halilovic gave an instruction to Dzankovic and the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have problems already with the language of 7(3) where we have the word "to punish." And you spoke about the material ability to punish. I think that's something impossible for a military leader because we have a division of powers, and he can only start investigations and he can only report to -- yes. And thus, I think the Prosecution made reference to all the available tools for Mr. Halilovic. Wouldn't you agree that disciplinary measures do not suffice; however, one would have to refer to the manuals in place, what is expected from a superior to do in a certain scenario. And in Hadzihasanovic we had a long analysis about these manuals and, indeed, came to the conclusion that there must be a possibility as you, in your words, material ability to report and -- or to start investigation. That's what's the manual says. Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect I agree with the proposition as I understand it to be that in a military context it won't be required of a -- of a general to hold the trial himself or to perform all of the steps. What may be required of the general will vary -- of the military officer will vary depending upon the structures that his army has in place for him to follow and whether he followed those in good faith. Of course the Tribunal will never be bound simply to accept that because he followed particular procedures that that necessarily suffices because the evidence may, in a given case, cast a different light upon it. But in the normal run of events and in this case one would appropriately look to what was the mechanism which the army had provided to investigate these crimes and what did it require of Sefer Halilovic in the circumstances. So that the question was: Was it open to him? What role did he have -- now, this is -- in a sense I've jumped forward to another element of the offence here. So I'm dealing with this -- I'll be clear, I will deal with the question, but I'm only focusing at this time on whether these matters prove he's in effective control or not. In other words, whether you can infer from what he did that he is in effective control as opposed to whether what he did was sufficient at a later time if proved to be in effective control. Those are different questions.;. Frankly they were raised obliquely by Your Honour yesterday -- I wouldn't say obliquely, they were raised by the question that Your Honour asked yesterday. That's correct. I'll make comments about evidence in that regard, if I may, I hope it's responsive to your question. I'll welcome being stopped if it's not. But it's saying that in a given case, evidence would be -- evidence of how a person responded to a situation may be admissible in a variety of ways, depends upon the case. In this case what is alleged by the Prosecutor is that Halilovic responded in the way he did because he's in effective control, because he's the de facto -- he's the de facto commander or de jure commander as was the case. Because he was a commander that's why he gave the instruction that he did to investigate. In other words, you can draw an inference from his actions that he, in fact, is the commander. That's the way they put it in relation to count -- to the first element. Of course the Prosecution case is you can infer that he's acknowledged his duties, but the Prosecution criticise how far he went. That's the way they put the case. But what the Defence says at this stage is it would not be safe -- I'll take it a step back. It was open to the Trial Chamber to make the finding that they did at paragraph 746 where they made the finding that what Halilovic did does not signify command responsibility or effective control, does not show that he had a material ability to punish or in the more focused way that Your Honour, Judge Schomburg, proposed that he did not have the material ability to investigate in the way that a commander would. What he had and what Halilovic did -- and it's important we think to appreciate the facts that occurred here. Halilovic had his team a representative of the military security services who was subject to his command within the structure of the inspection team. There is no doubt that that individual was subordinated to Halilovic within the team, but the military security service is not severable. Dzankovic was just one member of that team. Dzankovic had already commenced the investigation by the time Halilovic spoke to him and that's quite clear on the evidence, I'm not referring to pages here,, but it's uncontroversial that he had done so. So that what Halilovic did in speaking to Dzankovic was important but was not evidence of the effective control. The effect of what Halilovic did was to liberate Dzankovic from other duties in the inspection team, other roles he might have, and leave him free to do his job as an SVB member working with the SVB other people in the 6th Corps from the command, the command also linked to the 1st Corps back in Sarajevo, and to play his part in a large investigation which we say was a good investigation, and we take issue with the Prosecutor's claims that it was somehow segmented or to be treated as different parts. It was one investigation which Halilovic fully supported. What Halilovic did was to say: Continue with your investigation, I'll lend my moral support to the investigation. He expressed outrage about what had happened, said I am not behind that, and specifically approved, contrary to the submissions made yesterday, specifically approved Halilovic -- sorry, that Dzankovic should work with the MUP, with the civilian police, a member of whom was present at the time that Halilovic said what he said. So that Halilovic's response shows firstly moral rectitude; secondly, a correct attitude to allowing his -- the subordinate he has in his own team to participate in the investigation; and thirdly, encouraging him to do what he had to do. When Halilovic did that he must have known, because he was a senior officer and well familiar with army structures, that the SVB once activated and with jurisdiction would be pursuing this matter. And therefore Halilovic's actions are not explicable as the actions that only a commander could take. They do not add to the inference the Prosecution contends for here. Your Honours, that was a lengthy speech, and I understand that in some respects I went beyond the terms of the question, but it's because I'm seeking to in addressing this to deal with question 4 that was posed to the Defence by the questions from this Bench. And those questions focused upon how do we, as the Defence, respond to the allegation, the Dzankovic instruction, plus the Delic order later on means that Halilovic had effective control. We respond to it in steps. We say, first of all, that Halilovic's instruction does not show that he was in effective control. For reasons I've already articulated we say that, and now furthermore we draw the -- perhaps illustrate it by saying many people could, if you like, instigate an inspection that way, simply by telling the SVB, the military security service, there is a reasonable possibility of a crime in Grabovica. Once that was done you will see that -- again here we plunge right into the detail of the trial in a way that's awkward on appeal but I will do it. Exhibit 137 is the rules of the military security service, Articles 39, 40, and 41 of that make it quite clear and the Trial Chamber referred to these expressly that the military security service has full jurisdiction to investigate these crimes and has to do so once they have a "reasonable suspicion" of that crime. So Halilovic must have known that there was an investigation in place already and what he did was to augment that in a morally acceptable way but without betraying or suggesting that he was in effective control of the troops. The very terms of what he said is Namik, I am not behind that. Your Honours, we're protected somewhat by the finding of the Court here. This matter was expressly the subject of a finding at paragraph 746. And the Tribunal having anxiously considered all that evidence must be found to have come to that conclusion. The instruction to Dzankovic is an instruction, and I'll put this in more formal terms, has consistent -- with his role as head of the inspection team rather than his role as commander of Operation Neretva 93 the order didn't establish any change or chain of command or alter the relationship between Halilovic and the killers. Dzankovic was not in the chain of command at all with those killers, and the power he exercised was simply that of the inspection team and it's similar to the power that a Chief of Staff might have. Now, you can postulate a Chief of Staff who found out about crimes, doubtless he would tell the SVB go and investigate. That would not place the Chief of Staff in the line of command -- in the chain of command with those troops. And indeed one would hope that a Chief of Staff would do that. Supposing a Chief of Staff found out about crimes by a commander or those under the commander, one would hope he would approach the security services and say go and investigate. Your Honours, finally I comment -- my learned friend, Mr. Mettraux, has pointed out to me that the in the higher command post the accused Von Leeb I don't have the reference to this, but I'll refer to it now. Now, the Court noted that the possibility of the exercise of some powers does not imply that he has all such powers. In this case we would say that even if you found that the power that Halilovic found within the inspection team was of some significance it's not enough to create a position of effective control. Thus, we say that the Trial Chamber considered all -- all the relevant evidence, the substance of the situation. The Defence final brief considered this and this may assist at paragraph 617 to 713 and the Trial Chamber in the judgement at paragraph 653 to 659. The SVB, we say, we're the competent organ, and they were already the competent organ before Halilovic even found out about the crime, but as soon as he found out of course he did -- he did what he had to do. I want to deal with one other matter. It may be a little peripheral but it seems to have been raised by the Prosecution yesterday in submissions, and that is that there was an allegation made that a member of the inspection team had actually blocked the investigation in some way. Now, that evidence ought to be discounted here by: It didn't feature as a matter of importance in the judgement or in Prosecution's submissions at trial. What occurred there, Your Honour, was that there was a fourth-hand hearsay piece of suggestion that Mr. Karic had blocked the investigation in some way, had ordered no progress to take place. That evidence was to be found of Mr. Eminovic and it required the following chain to happen. Eminovic said that the military policeman Saric, not called, had heard from soldiers, not called, that Karic had given an instruction that nothing be done. That's the strength of it. That allegation was picked up in a number of exhibits. I believe it's referred to in Exhibit 215, and I acknowledge, although I can't find them, that there are two others to which it's referred. However, Dzankovic and Karic were both called to give evidence. This proposition was not put to them and not proved through them. So the live evidence at trial did not demonstrate any such blocking at all and it was incumbent if this was a significant part of the Prosecution case it had to be proved through the live witnesses that actually came at third-hand piece of information, perhaps relayed in good faith by witness Eminovic, was not accepted by the witness Dzankovic and -- I'm sorry, there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could the Defence refresh in our memory a little bit more regarding the Von Leeb case. Was this case which discussed the role of a staff officer in contrast to a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm instructed that, yes, it is in part, but, Your Honour, would it be appropriate for me to defer the further answer to that question? Mr. Mettraux will be addressing you in perhaps half an hour's time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that's the response in relation to the Dzankovic order and the situation that applied at the time when Halilovic did what he did. I turn now to the effect of the Delic order here. Our submission about that is that as to the first element of command responsibility, the Delic order adds precisely nothing and cannot do so. Its analytical reference could be, and we say it has no relevance to the third element, but it's capable of being relevant to the third element or at least an order like that could be, in case it might be said when considering the third element that a person was given further weapons or further assistance to carry out their duties, but even with that further assistance did not do so. In this case we say well that's not proved. But to use a post facto order like this to demonstrate effective control at the time of the crimes is, we'd submit generally speaking, would not be permitted. There may be the occasional situation where it would be as a matter of evidence but not in this case. I'll deal with that in just a moment. So the Delic order itself -- initially we say that effective control is pursuant to the Hadzihasanovic decision at paragraph 55 is to be assessed at the time of the crimes, and therefore, the relationship between Mr. Halilovic and the perpetrators has to -- falls to be assessed at that time. The duty to punish, therefore, arises by virtue of the relationship that exists at that time. And, Your Honours, this order came significantly after that time it arrives -- according to the evidence of Hodzic arrived on the 13th of the 9th and we submit that, therefore, is a post facto order. Therefore, it's functionally -- sorry, it's formally irrelevant it could not augment the power of Halilovic in terms of his effective control at the time of the crimes. Now, evidence like this may be used in an evidentiary way in a given case. So an order which had addressed Halilovic as commander of Neretva 93 and told him: Please investigate the troops under your command and control. Then although it didn't change his position, it may evidence his position. So if he's referred to by Delic as the commander at a later time, the Trial Chamber may have been entitled to use it in that way but it didn't do that. The order of Delic didn't refer to Halilovic as the commander of anything. It didn't refer to any operation Neretva or Neretva 93 or the IKM and it did not suggest any command role for Halilovic. And it was also addressed to somebody who was in the chain of command, namely, the commander of the 6th Corps. Furthermore, the terms of that order -- sorry, so perhaps to finish that point. What we submit is that, although sometimes a post facto order might be evidence, this particular order will not suffice in that way. Of course, the conclusion that overlies all of this is that the Trial Chamber looked at this order and it was open to the Trial Chamber to take the view that it did not augment the effective control of Halilovic. That's why the re-trial is such a difficult issue. I've here been arguing on the Prosecution's ground because I'm contending that it cannot be used in that way in any way. But on appeal when there's an acquitted accused, all we need to show is that it was open to the Trial Chamber to assess this as a matter of evidence, and that's what they did do; and therefore, the Prosecution hasn't shown that it was not open to them in that way. The Prosecution have asserted without any evidence that Halilovic disobeyed this order, but we say there is no proof of that at all that he disobeyed. The fact that the Prosecution didn't lead specific evidence of obedience does not mean that Halilovic disobeyed; and in that regard, we point to you that Delic himself was withdrawn as a witness by the Prosecution. And that if the Prosecution wished to lead evidence or seek an inference that Halilovic disobeyed this order, then it was incumbent on them to prove it or not just to assert it on appeal or indeed at trial. And by withdrawing Delic, the Prosecution have placed themselves in a position of evidence where it was well and truly open to the Judge not to have regard to this order. In summary, therefore, the Prosecution failed to demonstrate that this order has an impact upon the first element, nor -- and what we say is that they fail in their own ground because they don't establish that it could be used but this is an appeal against an acquittal and it's up to -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Morrissey, I would like to ask you to slow down in order to enable the interpreters to provide a proper translation to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will endeavour to comply in the best way that I can, and I apologise for the habitual speediness of this submission. Your Honour, in summary, therefore, with respect to the Delic order, it's a -- it's a post facto order, it did not add to the chain of command, the terms of the order are conditional in nature and you'll recall it uses the terms "if true," thereby not obliging Halilovic to do anything unless certain conditions were met. The Prosecution, of course, did not establish that those conditions were met and didn't try to in any way. It's also to be noted that at the time when Delic sent this order, that he must have been unaware of the proposals made by the SVB to investigate the crime. So Mr. Dzankovic at Exhibit 215, which is explicitly referred to in the judgement, made a careful and thorough assessment of what should be done to investigate the crime. He said we should form a mixed team, we should work with the civilian police, we should have a judge an investigate -- I can't recall now the terms of it, but effectively an investigative judge, may have been military prosecutor, may have been investigative judge, and we must take certain crime scene steps, and in short it was a very good and sensible proposal. That was filed or sent to his superiors on the 13th, and effectively, it crossed with the Delic order. Delic's order should be treated -- and no doubt was treated by the Trial Chamber and should have been treated in this way as nothing much more than an exhortation to those in Herzegovina to do what could be done, that it didn't create any specific powers in Halilovic which could augment his status as having effective control. And that is, of course, leaving aside the Hadzihasanovic objection here which we say just can't be used in that way later on. And it would be a wonderful way -- or it would create wonderful anomalies in the law if one could impose command responsibility on a person by appointing them after the event and thus wishing upon them responsibility for crimes which they were simply unconnected. Just as a final comment there, the Prosecution referred to the Exhibit 130, the inspection team report. But as was raised in questions posed by the Tribunal -- by the Appeals Chamber yesterday, it's quite clear that at the time of that inspection team report everyone knew, Delic, Jasarevic, Alispahic, Halilovic, everybody knew at that time that there was an investigation in place and there are numerous exhibits which demonstrate the course that investigation was taking. It was a good investigation and it was on foot at that time. It was not incumbent upon the inspection team to deal with that. One might think it was simply outside of their jurisdiction and outside of their relevance. The proposal -- so that's our submission about that. Finally we turn to the third part of part C. Now, part C was divided into three parts; the first two related allegedly to findings of the court, well, we say that the status as findings is uncertain. We say the Prosecution was entitled-- sorry, the Trial Chamber was entitled to make -- not to come to the findings that the Prosecution contends for. The last part which commences with paragraph 2.39 of the Prosecution's brief just lists a series of alleged material abilities. This has the vice that I referred to earlier on, the material ability to select troops, to issue warnings, to perform security assessments, and so on. But most of those abilities, Your Honour, in fact we would say all of them, do not indicate the relationship between Halilovic and the perpetrators that has to be established. They do not indicate or evidence or advance the chain of command between those. They are not evidence of command power. There are references -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm just concerned about time. Just excuse me and I'm going -- I would refer only to a couple of -- to a couple. We adopt what we said in our brief about this matter, but I would refer to the -- no, look, for time purposes I'm going to press on. It is said that he had a power -- that Halilovic had a power to engage -- to assign military police to the village, but the evidence just didn't support that. Your Honours, the Defence final trial brief at paragraph 696 analysed these matters, and when you consider the evidence about the military police, again we plunge deep into the trial record here and into the evidence, but the Prosecution in a sense in the abstract imposing duties without regard to the evidence. The evidence about the availability of the military police was that there were two companies, one in Konjic far away, one in Jablanica. The company's full strength was 76 men, they operated at that time with a strength of 60 men. And in terms of a daily availability of men, it was between 5 and 20. And the evidence of Nermin Eminovic on this topic was referred to explicitly by the Trial Chamber and that was the situation. Now the idea of sending those military police into the village in a display of force -- or that Halilovic had the power to do that is not established. Halilovic did not have power over the military police. He was not in the chain of command. He simply didn't have that power. It was said he could engage or he should -- he had the material ability to engage the civilian police to assist the investigation. He didn't have that command power, but to the extent that -- and to the extent that he could do it he could do so simply by proving what his -- what his SVB representative Dzankovic had already done. And so we refer in general to our brief in that regard and to the Defence trial brief at 697 to 701. And I shall now move on from that point. Your Honours, in conclusion that ground 1, sub 1, was an uneasy ground at all times because in the notice of appeal it was focused upon de facto commander status of Halilovic, and here on -- when the argument comes to be mounted and through the brief, it focused on a much broader concept. There is no de facto commander case left, although in reply it might be expected the Prosecution will say the de facto commander part is just an element of an all-embracing approach to effective control. It brings us back to that pleadings argument and it brings us back to the era under subsection B. The case beyond command we say was waived and it's no error to ignore it. But even if you admitted it, even if you fail to consider considered that new case of command now it still fails there would still be a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber at 752 and 746 still dealt with effective control as such and found that it was not established. That ground fails. The effect of that ground failing is the whole appeal fails in my respectful submission. Nevertheless, we turn to the other grounds. Would you just excuse me for a moment. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. There's now going to be distinct acceleration, Your Honours. Your Honours, ground 1 sub-2 dealt with Operation Neretva. I want to deal with that one as quickly as I can, but by explaining why it mattered because here we say the Prosecution are very artificial. The purpose of this evidence -- the purpose of the evidence about the operation was to establish a chain of command. Because Halilovic was not in the chain of command, was not proved to be and clearly wasn't, it was necessary for the Prosecution to show that there was some chain by which he did exercise effective control through command power over the perpetrators and that was the operation. Proving the existence, the name, and the significance of the operation were preliminary matters for the Prosecution, but they had to be proved because that was their path home. They had to prove those matters. It was necessary for them but not sufficient for them. Now, at trial the Prosecution we say did not prove that, Your Honours. It was a failure of evidence not a failure of focus by the Trial Chamber. The evidence about Zenica failed. It was proved it was no such operation there and Halilovic wasn't appointed to it despite the explicit allegations in the indictment. The Prosecution here are up against this problem, that the Trial Chamber followed the indictment very step by step through and dealt with the material facts that are alleged in it as they're obliged to do. Your Honours, we adopt our brief on that topic. The fact is the various combat operations which took place in Herzegovina in that time were not themselves proved to be conducted pursuant to that Operation Neretva. I will mention in particular that the Uzdol combats, as Exhibits 149 to 152, this is lengthy order analysis that has to go on to establish this, but it was done and we say it was accepted in the Uzdol case, that Enver Buza went into battle, he's the Prozor independent battalion went into battle pursuant to orders from the 6th Corps, not pursuant to Operation Neretva not from orders of Halilovic or at the behest of the IKM that's at Uzdol and one might say it's a little remote. But when you turn to the offending units who were subordinated to the Zulfikar unit, there you have a battle which had nothing to do with Operation Neretva, Operation Neretva 93 or the IKM or to Halilovic, but Exhibit 503, exhibits complete independence and you need to look at the terms of that as we've asked you to do in the final brief. It's apparent that Zulfikar Alispago having torn up the instruction he received from the inspection team as it was established in evidence, then drafted his own order which indicated: I have decided to attack along these axes, which indicated in a variety of ways that he was very much his own man and supporting -- sorry, and reporting back to Commander Delic, as he did do, as he did do, directly to Delic. So when the Trial Chamber made its findings that it was not persuaded that the combat operations had taken place pursuant to Operation Neretva, that was simply an evidentiary finding that was fully open to it. When you have regard to the notice of appeal now, you'll see that the notice had to construct out of that an implicit error of law. The error was not made explicitly so the Prosecution said it was implicit. It said in the notice of appeal that the Trial Chamber required the name to be proved as a pre-condition to conviction. But when you look in the notice -- when you look at the finding itself at paragraphs 175 and its important precursor paragraph 174, that error simply isn't made. And you have to deal with the error that's alleged by the Prosecutors, not by the, if you like, polished version that is now being put forward. In argument it was said this implicitly required proof of de jure and not a de facto relationship, but in establishing an operation -- well, it was open to the Trial Chamber to take the position that they did. Your Honours, what the evidence about Operation Neretva or Neretva 93 never did establish is, that it established a chain of command or that it involved the resubordination of the Zulfikar unit to Halilovic. And that's the key because it's through the Zulfikar unit, and only through that, that the Prosecution say Halilovic had effective control of the offenders. Of course, the Defence says there was another break at the level of Delalic himself, but in any event there was just no evidence that established that and on appeal the Prosecution have got to show you that it was incumbent on the Trial Chamber to accept that. We say not only was it open to doubt but that is what the evidence proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, Judge Schomburg has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I heard you very often speaking about Operation Neretva, and I think it was subground two of the Prosecution as regards the name of the operation. Can I take it that you also see it as irrelevant how the operation was called and the parties agree what the operation at stake was? That the name, as such, is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the parties are not meeting -- are not meeting properly on this issue, so we don't agree because we attribute different significance to different things. The Defence doesn't concede that the operation was called Operation Neretva. The situation was this: The Trial Chamber accepted that there were multiple combat operations and in terms you will see in paragraphs 174 and 175 and thereafter at paragraphs 727 and 737, and I believe in a later paragraph as well, but those ones at least make it quite clear the Trial Chamber dealt with combat operations. Included among those operations must be Operation Vrdi 93. The Trial Chamber was in doubt that that operation Vrdi 93 took place under or under the auspices of or connected to Operation Neretva or Operation Neretva 93. The failure as to the name of -- of -- of what is said to be Operation Neretva 93 is a matter of significance because it reflects doubt as to what this operation was. And what the Defence says is that whether you deal with it at the level of the name or at another level, Operation Neretva is a concept that doesn't establish what the Prosecution hoped. It doesn't establish the chain of command or an ability to exercise effective control of Halilovic of the perpetrators. It was combat operations collectively, which the Trial Chamber found had taken place. The Trial Chamber was clearly not prepared to make a finding that Operation Neretva, whatever it was, ever constituted an effective military structure which imposed a chain of command. That's why we say, although I do appreciate the sense of Your Honour's question, we do maintain that the failure to prove the name is symptomatic of a general failure by the Prosecution to say what on earth Operation Neretva or Neretva 93 actually was. And what appears to be the situation is that the Trial Chamber were not prepared to make definitive findings on that because the evidence was too poor. The evidence didn't support it. What the evidence really showed is that Operation Neretva was a work in progress. It's referred to sporadically and more often than not after the event. The name on the map which is the contemporary reference, it's Exhibit 131 I think, is Operation Neretva and there's no 93. Yes, it may seem like a small detail but in a military setting you would think and you would expect that if this concept, this Operation Neretva 93 had any existence in reality, that it would be quite clear what it was, when it started, who was its commander, what were its staffs, what units were subordinated to it. No evidence of that, not up to today. And that's why the Trial Chamber didn't make definitive findings about it. What it was entitled to find is there was combat and the offenders committed their crimes in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This gave me a far better understanding of para 175 of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. Very well. We turn now, Your Honour, to ground 1.3, this is the IKM ground. Your Honour, this ground and my address on this ground will also attempt to deal with question 3. I'll make some brief comments after that about subground four. Subgrounds five and six we are going to rely on our brief and Mr. Mettraux will then commence to deal with the submissions as to the remaining grounds. Now, the IKM ground arises against a similar confusion about background -- so Your Honour's question about the Operation Neretva reveals what we say is a symptom of this brief. It's not a conscious -- I don't mean this term in an insulting way, it's a misrepresentation of what this case was about. At the time, paragraph 175 was important to understanding how -- what the significance of the operation was, it was the chain of command. Now we turn to the IKM. The Prosecution allege an overly formal approach to it, but it's they who are taking an overly formal approach to it and we'll demonstrate that now. We need to show why the IKM evidence mattered and the reason it mattered was because this was a case where the Prosecution said, Halilovic was the commander of an operation and in order to prove that, we'll find that there was a command post from which it was commanded. Now, this could have assisted the Prosecutor as evidence if it were proved that Halilovic had a proper forward command post, as Mr. Karic said in evidence, with all its powers and prerogatives, with an order creating it with the staffs with the powers. If it had those powers, that may assist to draw an inference. We say it would be an inference of de jure power. In other words, if Halilovic isn't the commander, what's he doing running a command post, that would be a legitimate way to argue. That's why the Prosecution were keen to establish the IKM. But it has to be remembered that an IKM is a product of military doctrine. And its powers, the powers that come from it, or the powers that it has are products of military doctrine. Of course, in a given case, it might be established that a particular -- well, that's what I say about that at this stage. When the evidence came to be analysed, that's not how it worked out -- I'm sorry. Your Honours, the use of the term IKM must have been tempting to the Prosecution as investigators because they would see references to IKM and knowing their military doctrine would say: Aha, this could mean something about the nature of the military operation; however, that's not the case. Once the evidence came to be considered, it turned out that the IKM was not really an IKM at all. The Trial Chamber considered the substance of what happened at that office and the evidence proved that the inspection team established an office in Jablanica of two rooms and that's where they went about their work. Mr. Karic and Mr. Dzankovic gave very clear evidence about this. They said we used to call it an IKM but it wasn't really one. Now, that evidence was able to be accepted by the Trial Chamber and it obviously was accepted by the Trial Chamber. So what looked like a forward command post from which he might be able to draw inferences turned out from the evidence to let the Prosecution down. There is a lot -- between paragraphs 211 and 221 of the judgement you will see a very pain-staking and careful analysis of the facts on that topic. There was -- so de jure, therefore, the Prosecution case on this point collapsed completely in the face of that evidence. Now, in order not to appear to be overly formal about it, the Trial Chamber also considered the evidence of what was done at this office and to see whether or not perhaps it lent some glamour or some power or some authority or -- to use Judge El Mahdi comments -- some clout to the inspection team and its members; but the evidence failed the Prosecution there too. Never did membership of the IKM or attendance at the so-called IKM lend authority or gravitas to any action by a member of the inspection team. It was open to the Trial Chamber to connect that and I make this point, too, this will be the final point I make on this topic. That the IKM -- I'm calling it the IKM as the Trial Chamber did as a convenient way of describing it as Karic did and the inspection team did as a convenient way of explaining it. It's the Prosecutors who wish to attribute some significance to the use of that term, not the Defence. The Prosecutors hoped to establish that this was a forward command post, but the activities that went on there were not command activities. It lent no glamour, no support, it had no effect. And certainly, it lent no support to a connection between to Halilovic and the perpetrators. In particular, it's not shown that the perpetrators knew anything about this institution. What the Trial Chamber pointed out was, so far as those individuals referred to an IKM, it was the command at Zuka's base, which was at a different location in Donji Jablanica some kilometres away. The officers of the inspection team called IKM for jargon -- were right in the middle of Jablanica. The Zuka base was kilometres away and that's what the perpetrators referred to and that's where the perpetrators went. They didn't go to this IKM and had nothing to do with the crimes. So to conclude this ground, in formal terms the notice of appeal claims that the Trial Chamber imposed a precondition and in effect erred in law by requiring the Prosecution to prove that this was a formal IKM but that's turning inside out what the Trial Chamber did. The Trial Chamber did no more than to make a finding of fact in direct response to a material fact pleaded in the indictment. The Trial Chamber found this piece of evidence was of no significance, and that was the importance of it. Your Honours, I refer to the Defence trial brief at 258 to 259 in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Morrissey, you have 20 minutes left. You told us that Mr. Mettraux was going to take the floor also, so please bear in mind our time constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are now borne in mind. I'll conclude by saying that subground four and the argument put there are subsumed in the argument that was put in subground one concerning the Delic order and the Dzankovic instructions. I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The time left for the Defence we would wish to address the three questions, question number 4, question number 6, and question number 7, which were addressed to the Defence by the Appeals Chamber. If time permits, some other matters may also be discussed by the defence. But before I start, I would wish perhaps to add to the answer given by my lead counsel in relation to questions from Judge Schomburg and Judge Meron. Judge Schomburg has indicated a certain discomfort with the expression "material ability" as a proper term to describe the adequacy of what is relevant to effective control, and this is indeed a position if indeed that is the position of Your Honour which we share. We understand the position under international law in relation to this issue to be this. The question is not whether any other steps or any other measures could be taken in addition to those that have been taken by a commander, as may be the case. They are always additional measures. There will always be additional steps, additional measures that could be taken by a commander. The real test is this: Considering the measures taken by a commander in the circumstances, was this conduct reasonable in the circumstances? The Defence submit that the discretion which a commander has in relation to those matters is his, not that of the Court which would be required at a later stage to assess whether he followed the proper conduct. And perhaps to assist in that matter, I would like to refer to a decision of the Supreme Court of Israel in a matter which we must consider is slightly different. The question that was asked of the Supreme Court was whether security measures taken by a commander in the field were proper or not and reasonable, and this is what the Supreme Court said: "In exercising judicial review, we do not make ourselves into security experts. We do not replace the military commander's security considerations with our own. We take no position on the way security issues are handled. Our job is to maintain boundaries and to guarantee the existence of conditions that restrict the military commander's discretion because of the important security aspects in which the commander's decision is grounded. We do not, however, replace the commander's discretion with our own. We insist upon the legality of the military commander's exercise of discretion and that it falls into the range of reasonableness determined by the relevant legal norms applicable to the issue." We submit, Your Honour, that the position is identical under international law and in domestic law to the extent that international law refer to that body of law. Yesterday, questions were raised both by I believe both by Judge Shahabuddeen and by Judge Meron as to whether in a particular circumstance or circumstances a commander would act properly if he delegated the responsibility of investigating the matter, an allegation of crime, to a subordinate. The answer to the Prosecution was: Well, our position was no. There is -- if you want, a super-obligation, that goes beyond that. Well, with respect this is not the position under international law. I will cite only one case, this is the Ford versus Garcia case. It's a US case federal court case which refers to many source -- many interesting sources of international law. And in this judgement the Court said that: "The commander may fulfil his duty to investigate and punish wrong-doers, if he delegates this duty to a responsible subordinate. The commander has a right to assume that the assignment entrusted to a responsible subordinate will be properly executed. On the other hand, the duty to investigate and punish will not be fulfilled if the commander knows or reasonably should know that the subordinate will not carry out his assignment in good faith or if the commander impedes or frustrate the investigation." The further questions which were raised in relation to this matter, and perhaps I will give the reference for the assistance of Your Honours, is US federal court of Florida, Ford versus Garcia, and it's a judgement of 3 November of 2000, the case is also cited with approval in the ICRC customary study in volume 2, 661. The further question which was raised yesterday by Your Honours in relation to delegation of responsibility for investigation was whether a commander would be entitled to assume that the investigation is going according to plans, and again the answer is yes. Unless the commander receives explicit or clear information that something is going wrong with the investigation, he's entitled to believe that this is going according to course. And I refer to the high command case where it is said the following: "He," the commander, "has a right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed." Judge Meron also raised the question, and we promised to come back to it and I shall do immediately, about the Von Leeb case. The Von Leeb case was in the part of the high command case in which a number of pronunciation were made in relation to the duties and the specificities of the responsibilities of the Chief of Staff. The reference, however, which we would wish to make today is to a different part, and I would read it for the benefit of the Chamber in a minute. The point which was made by the Tribunal, the US Tribunal in Nuremberg at the time was that the executive power with which Mr. Von Leeb had been endowed limited his ability to issue orders. They were limited to orders in the field of operational matters but not administrative matters. The relevance of this was that the Tribunal found that he could not be held responsible in relation to matters and competencies which fell outside of the scope of his responsibilities. And perhaps I shall read the relevant paragraph. It is the high command case at page 554 and 555 of the green series. It says this: "Executive power at the beginning of the Russian campaign was conferred directly upon the army commanders and the commanders of the army group rear areas. It was provided, however, that the Commander-in-Chief of an army group might issue orders to his subordinates in the field of executive powers. In other words, his authority in this field was more in the nature of a right to intervene than a direct responsibility. This power to intervene followed the general pattern of his command authority over subordinate units. Nevertheless, authority and responsibility as to many administrative matters were directly vested in Von Leeb's subordinate. As stated his function was operational. Many administrative duties had been left to his subordinated armies and his army group area. He and his staff alike would have the right to assume that the commanders entrusted with search administrative function would see to their proper execution. Under such conditions it must be accepted that certain details of activities within the sphere of his subordinates would not be brought to his attention." This, Your Honour, we said was relevant. The Prosecution is trying to bring into the fold of command responsibility. What we say was, in fact, matters relevant to Mr. Halilovic's responsibility as the team leader of an inspection team. The mandate of the inspection team did not include any duties or obligation as regard the prevention or punishment of crime, and the orders which have been referred by Your Honour in the questions, the order of Mr. Delic of the 12th of September or the instruction of Mr. Halilovic of the 9th of September, did not change this situation at all, nor did it displace or reorganise the chain of command in any ways. Perhaps because question 4 has been covered quite extensively by my colleague, I will start with the second of Your Honour's question, which was the issue of mens rea, and the question was as follows: How does Sefer Halilovic respond to the Prosecution's contention based on the language of the Celebici appeal judgement that he should have known that soldiers of the 9th Brigade were going to commit murders in Grabovica? We submit that there are many relevant reasons why the situation in this case did not meet the relevant standard of mens rea. I will summarize them for Your Honours. The first reason and the first reason why the ground of appeal itself should be rejected is, in effect, the Prosecution is asking of you for an advisory opinion. They have withdrawn the allegation -- the submissions made in the notice that the Trial Chamber had erred. What they have now asked you to do is to make a general finding for the benefit, we suppose, of another trial and have asked you to make that finding. Well, this type of advisory opinion falls beyond the corrective jurisdiction of the Tribunal, but it also reveals that the Prosecution's appeal within any case be incapable of succeeding in the absence of what they say is a finding on that point. The second matter, and again this may appear technical, but this is revealing of a pattern in this case we submit, is the allegation now raised of a submission now made by the Prosecution that knowledge of an alleged criminal reputation of the 9th Brigade would have been sufficient to provide notice of the crime, is a new allegation and I will come back to that. I simply at this stage draw Your Honours attention to paragraph 15 of the indictment. The third reason why this ground of appeal should be rejected is that contrary to the allegation made by the Prosecution both in its appeal brief and yesterday in oral submission, the Trial Chamber, in fact, made an express finding to the effect that the Prosecution had failed to establish that alleged reputation. And I will read to you this finding. The fourth reason why this ground of appeal should be rejected and perhaps most fundamental of all is that the Prosecution, indeed, failed to establish the reputation which they alleged in the indictment and failed to establish that Mr. Halilovic had knowledge, whether in the form of knew or had reason to know, of any such reputation. The last matter we submit which would justify the rejection of this ground of appeal is the fact that the Prosecution has not turned its mind to each and every element that constitute the mens rea necessary under Article 7(3), in particular neither at trial nor during this appeal has the Prosecution attempted to prove what we say is a requirement of customary international law that the failure attributed to a superior must be intentional, deliberate, and akin to acquiescence. I will cite a number of cases in support of that proposition. Your Honour, I will move very quickly on the first issue, the issue of proper pleading. I would simply draw your attention again to paragraph 15 of the indictment. There is no allegation, no independent allegation that the fact or the knowledge of this alleged reputation in itself would have been relevant and sufficient. I also draw Your Honours attention to paragraph 523 of the judgement itself which summarize, in effect, the Prosecution case on that point. I would finally draw your attention to the submissions of lead counsel Morrissey during the final arguments at trial, when Mr. Morrissey in a way threw the gauntlet at the Prosecution asking them tell us at last when they allege Mr. Halilovic required the necessary notice and when they say his duty to act was triggered. And I will read that passage to you. "And it will be interesting to see, Your Honours, when the time for reply comes whether the Prosecution then seek to advance a time and wait and see whether they, do or they don't, a time at which the duty to prevent, that is, was imposed on Halilovic. They haven't done it up until now, and we'll see when it is they do with an hour to go in the trial." It will be interesting to Your Honour to note that the Prosecution did not do so in it's reply. Now the situation on appeal is this: The Prosecution is blaming the Trial Chamber for failure which is only its own. The next submission that the Prosecution has made is that the Trial Chamber had made no finding as regard the reputation, the alleged criminal reputation of the troops, in particular the 9th Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mettraux, you have five minutes left to finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. The suggestion by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't be too hard on the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It will be a difficult balance. Well, the passage I would like to read or the comment or the finding that I would like to read to Your Honour is the summary of the Trial Chamber findings which is to be found on the transcript, on the record of the trial which is, with Your Honour, it's the transcript of the 16th of November, 2005, page 6, it's the transcript of the judgement. The Trial Chamber said this: "The Trial Chamber has been provided with evidence concerning the nature of the 9th and 10th Brigades, referred to in the indictment as having notorious reputations of being criminal and uncontrolled. The evidence shows that members of both brigades not only demonstrated a lack of discipline but also took civilians to dig trenches at the front line and committed thefts and other forms of misappropriation. However, the trial found that these misconducts were not comparable to the crimes committed in Grabovica." And I stop here for a second. The requirement under the law of this Tribunal, in particular in the Naletilic and Krnojelac's appeals judgement is that the notice relevant to charges of murder or to charges of any other crime would be similar in character to the crimes charged against the accused. The Trial Chamber goes on to say: "The Trial Chamber notes in this respect the testimony of 1st Corps commander Vahid Karavelic, who while knowing of the breaches of discipline and the previous behaviour of members of those brigades, said that it never occurred to him that they might commit atrocity against civilians in Grabovica." That finding, Your Honour, the summary of what the Trial Chamber found is consistent, both with the evidence which was led at trial, with the finding of the Trial Chamber in the judgement, and this finding has not been appealed by the Prosecution. They are simply pretending that it does not exist. Another matter relevant to the reputation, and that's -- I will draw Your Honours' attention to the Hadzihasanovic trial judgement paragraph 1543, 1748 to 1750 and the Sabra and Chatila report, the Barak report, which makes an interesting point. They note that the reputation to the relevant -- to notice would be reputation of the same group of men who have committed the crimes or who are alleged to have committed the crimes. In this particular case only one man, Mr. Mustafa Hota, was identified as having had any prior disciplinary problems prior to taking part in crimes in Grabovica. The problem with Mr. Hota are several. The first thing and perhaps most important here is that Mr. Hota was not even a de jure member of the 9th Brigade at the times where the crimes were committed. He only became a member of that unit on the 15th of September, 1993. There could therefore have been no notice of perhaps a problematic individual being sent to Herzegovina. There is also no evidence that Mr. Halilovic was aware of problems with Mr. Hota or that he would be sent to Herzegovina. The test, Your Honour, and I will be brief on this, is that there must have been an indication of the substantial likelihood that crimes would be committed. It must be the crime of murder, and the crime in question must have been about to be committed. That means that the commander must have been informed that steps had been taken to prepare or plan those crimes. The evidence, Your Honour, and perhaps I will conclude with this with your leave, is that there was simply no evidence to prove that the crimes had either been foreseen or foreseeable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry if I interrupt you, Mr. Mettraux. But we could grant you an extra ten minutes because the Prosecution yesterday had some extra time. So you have ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Swiss time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's a Swiss without the watch, so I will be under the guidance of the Appeals Chamber on that front. Simply to indicate to Your Honours that the evidence never supported a case of notice in relation to the alleged reputation of those troops, also for another reason, simply the evidence. The evidence was led in this court was as follows. None of the villagers tried to leave the village. None of the villagers who the Prosecution claims should have been extremely frightened about those troops, none of them left. The survivors who came in this courtroom to testify did not suggest that they felt at the time that there was such a risk for them. The evidence of the corps commander of the 1st Corps was also given -- he gave the same version, and I have to read it through the citation from the Trial Chamber itself. One of the killers also appeared in this courtroom as a witness for the Prosecution. He again testified that he had no indication and no reason to believe that something like this would happen. A member of the inspection team, Mr. Karic, was also asked about this and perhaps his evidence is incredibly relevant on that point and it's the evidence of the 2nd of June, 2005, page 8 and 12. It's not a lack of foresight due to negligence, Your Honour. Mr. Karic and other members of the inspection team went into the village to verify and what they found is that there were no problems with the troop, and again I draw your attention to the transcript of the 2nd of June of 2005, page 8 to 12 of 13. The Prosecution in its appeals brief relies on the evidence of one witness, Mr. Jasarevic, the head of the military security service, who gave evidence in court, and claimed that based on his evidence, as referred in the appeal brief paragraph 325, footnote 274, page 63, that he gave evidence to the effect that the crimes were foreseeable. Well, I will let Your Honour read the relevant paragraph that the Prosecution said for yourself, but the evidence of the witness on that point was this and this is the evidence of 2nd March, 2005, page 35 to 36, this is Mr. Jasarevic. "Of course I couldn't assume that that unit could do anything like that." And then he adds: "Yes, I was shocked, absolutely, when I found out about the crime." There was simply no evidence from any witnesses that anyone had foreseen that such a crime would happen and certainly no evidence that Mr. Halilovic had any such notice. I take perhaps this opportunity to answer another question of Judge Schomburg of yesterday when he asked the Prosecution whether they believed that there may be an issue of self-incrimination if a superior were to be charged for both failure to prevent and punish and whether it could create in a way a disincentive to reporting. Perhaps we can assist in at least in a limited way. We understand the position to be this: Should the commander be charged, indeed, with failure to prevent and failure to punish and should he act in such a way that he reports the crime or he otherwise contributed to an investigation, we submit that this evidence would be directly relevant and extremely important to an inference as to the state of mind of that person. A commander would actively take steps to punish or to see to the fact that crimes be investigated, there would be a mountain to climb for the Prosecution to claim that that same commander knew of the possibility or the likelihood of crime, I should say, that he did nothing to prevent those crimes. We believe that at the least, Your Honour, this evidence would be directly relevant to rebut any allegation that he possessed the required mens rea as regard the failure to prevent and that he intended deliberately and consciously not to act. And that would be the next point which I would like to turn to. There is a wealth of authorities under international law which I will simply cite as a pack. The High Command, the Hostage case, the Flick case, the Jespen case, the Toyoda case, even Strugar at paragraph 439, Musema at paragraph 131, the Koster case from the Vietnam, the final report of the Commission of Experts on this Tribunal, all of them agreed that one of the elements of great importance to the state of mind of superior responsibility is the proof that the failure of the commander was intentional, deliberate, and that it may be regarded as either acquiescence or approval with the crime. One perhaps of the best example of that position is the one of the Bagilishema Appeals Chamber in its judgement at paragraph 35 where it says that it must be demonstrated that the superior either by -- I mean the attempt to discharge his duty as superior either by deliberately failing to perform them or by culpably or wilfully discharging them. As you will see the language of some of the World War II cases go even further than that. And perhaps if I have, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've got another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will try to address some of the issues raised in relation to the fourth question in Your Honour's addendum to the Scheduling Order. Very briefly to say this in response to the suggestion that the orders of Mr. Delic and the instruction of Mr. Halilovic to Dzankovic are relevant to effective control. The first point we would like to raise is a point which I understood Judge Mr. Meron to do yesterday during the arguments of the Prosecution is the evidence that someone would get involved into an investigation, make a contribution to that investigation, would necessarily mean, we understand the Prosecution to claim this, it would necessarily mean that he has the material ability to contribute to punishing and preventing a crime and that he's therefore in effective control of the troops. This is wrong. The situation is this, it will be evidentially relevant only if that ability to contribute to the investigation or the punishment of the crime is the consequence of a relationship of superior and subordinate with the accused. The example which I think was used by Judge Meron yesterday was that a Prosecutor. It is an excellent one with respect and the same could be said about a police officer. A police officer can contribute, indeed, to investigating a criminal matter, and in a limited sense he will therefore have the material ability to contribute. But he would not be in a relationship of effective control with the troops. The reason for that may be found, in among other things, the Celebici appeals judgement and the Bagilishema appeals judgement again where there is a requirement that the person in question had the ability to exercise control over the troops. And that's a control, as Mr. Morrissey that must be exercised at the time when the crimes were committed. The Celebici Appeals Chamber 198 and Bagilishema paragraph 62.
