Turning to the Delic order, very briefly, we say that this order could not possibly be regarded as evidence of effective control. There are several reasons for that. The first one is that to the extent that this order would be indicative of any powers or authority, that would be the powers and authority of Mr. Delic himself. To the extent that an order is passed down the chain of command, the authority which is exercised is that of the commander or the officer which set -- which sent the order down in the first place. And an excellent example of that situation is the situation with Mr. Delic, another Mr. Delic in the Celebici case where the Chamber had to consider whether a number of orders which he had signed were evidence of effective control. The Trial Chamber at the time, and the matter was not otherwise overturned on appeal, said no it demonstrated a level of intermediate command where the authority which he exercised was merely the exercise of his own -- of the powers of his own superior. The second reason why this order of Mr. Delic is irrelevant to effective control, as Mr. Morrissey already pointed out, there is a requirement under international law of an existence of a chain of command between the perpetrators on the one hand and the accused on the other. It may be a formal legal military chain of command or it can be a de facto chain of command, and there I can simply take the time to mention the Celebici Appeals Chamber, 303; Kordic Trial Chamber, 416; Kajelijeli, 84, 85, adopting the position of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 773. The third reason why this order of Mr. Delic is irrelevant is that it did not endow Mr. Halilovic with any additional powers or authority. To the extent that it would be read as giving him additional obligations or different mandate, this mandate was not accompanied by any other means or resources. His ability to do something about it at all times remained the same, and it's very interesting, and Your Honour should remember the fact that this order was also sent, the same order to the commander of the 6th Corps, Mr. Gusic, who had those powers and we say the responsibility to take certain steps. The fourth matter in relation to that order is that with or without that order it would still remain to be proved that the level of authority which the Prosecution say Mr. Halilovic acquired through that order met the very high threshold of effective control. The order was considered by the Chamber, the Chamber said no. The fifth and last reason why this order is irrelevant has again been highlighted by Mr. Morrissey the time at which it was given. A commander may not be made the commander of a superior of troops ex post facto and perhaps in 20 seconds, with Your Honour's indulgence, concerning the Dzankovic's order, the first reason why this order is not relevant to effective control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: With pleasure, Your Honour. In three sentences the Dzankovic order did not create the relationship of authority between Mr. Halilovic and the perpetrators. At all times his responsibilities remained that of the leader of an inspection team. Mr. Dzankovic had no power over the perpetrators or otherwise upon the chain of command, and that all of the actions, including the order or the instructions to Mr. Dzankovic, were consistent and limited to the role and function of Mr. Halilovic as leader of the inspection team. I'm grateful to Your Honour for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mettraux. We are going to have a break, a 20-minute break, and we shall resume at quarter past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Kremer, you have the floor for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will reply firstly to the question reserved from yesterday asked by Judge Meron. It had two parts to it. The first part addressed how, if we prevailed on subgrounds two, three, and four of ground one, would it require the Appeals Chamber to conclude that the Trial Chamber erred in finding Halilovic to be commander of the operation. In answer to this specific question, we say that by requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt for the name of the operation, that is, Operation Neretva, and the establishment of a forward command post, the IKM, as well as using the failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish to conclude that no material -- that there was no material ability, the Trial Chamber committed a legal error, as we have alleged in the notice of appeal and discussed in our appeal brief and that the consequence of finding a legal error in respect of these three subgrounds, applying the Blaskic appeals judgement of paragraph 15, would permit the Appeals Chamber to apply the correct legal standard to the evidence. And the reason for that application would be because it is impossible to determine the weight that the Trial Chamber placed on those individual findings in respect of the major ground of appeal addressing effective control. As Mr. Morrissey properly pointed out, the facts in regard to effective control included not only the actions by Sefer Halilovic as head of the inspection team, but included as well all of the aspects surrounding the operation of the inspection team during the course of the operation. Dealing with the second question, Judge Meron raised a question about how the Prosecution's case was pleaded at trial, and he asked whether the Prosecution's case of effective control was based solely on command. And I interpret from the question that there's a concern about the fairness of the Prosecution's position on appeal. I want to say quite specifically that the Defence was always aware of the Prosecution's case and that the Prosecution's case was based on an allegation that Halilovic was the superior over subordinates who committed the crime and not solely on whether he was the commander of the operation. And the first document that proves this point is the indictment, which put the accused on notice that the allegations against him were based only on superior responsibility under Article 7(3). Material facts pleaded in the indictment support the allegation. Included are facts that he was appointed commander of the operation, but the indictment also included allegations of other material facts, showing that the accused was the superior because he had effective control over the subordinates. For example, in paragraphs 36 and 37, Halilovic's high-ranking and experienced authority are detailed, mentioning his chief of command staff, his deputy commander, senior officer, and experienced commander roles. Paragraphs 1, 3, and 4 discuss leadership and role of the inspection team, and paragraph 39, perhaps the most important reference under the concluding description -- excuse me for a moment. The superior responsibility section, 35 through 39, Sefer Halilovic demonstrated both formal de jure and de facto power by his command and control in military matters. In a manner consistent with the exercise of superior authority by issuing orders, instructions, and directives to the units, by ensuring the implementation of these orders, instructions, and directives, and bearing full responsibility for their implementation. He also assigned lines of attack and coordinated the combat activities of the units. He planned and was instrumental in the implementation of the military operations carried out by the units which took part in the Neretva 93 operation. In the decision of 17 February 2004, the Pre-Trial Chamber identifies the necessary material facts supporting the subordinate relationship in these paragraphs. It says at paragraph 15, by reference to superior/subordinate relationship effective control, in footnote 31, that these are the paragraphs that apply to defining the superior/subordinate relationship, and that was 1, 3, 4, 5, 35 through 39, and 43. Also the pre-trial brief at paragraph 172 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, did you read paragraph 38 of the indictment which says that: "At all times relevant to the charges in the indictment, by virtue of his position and authority as commander of the operation, he had effective control." So it seems to me that the accused would have been told there by the Prosecution that, true, the question was whether he had effective control, but only as stated here: "By virtue of his position and authority as commander." Now, it is true in paragraph 39 you referred to his having authority de jure and de facto, but are these perhaps more properly to be regarded as routes to his having command and control, there being a question as to whether the territorial army had evolved into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina by a process which might be regarded as not quite attractive of formal appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The allegation in paragraph 38 does allege by virtue of his position and authority as commander a de facto allegation. Paragraph 39 alleges a de facto commander allegation under the authority of the exercise of superior authority and, as I will take the Chamber to in a moment, a series of documents filed by the Defence during the course of the pre-trial and trial proceedings show that they were fully aware of the fact that the Crown's case was not based solely on the de facto commander position, but went beyond that to include superior authority. And the indictment paragraph 39 clearly suggests that the de facto power led to his superior -- was exercised in a manner consistent with his superior authority, which, our position is, is a different allegation than contained in paragraph 38 of the indictment. And the context of the military operations and the ABiH army is a factual backdrop to the interpretation of the superior responsibility that was alleged. Our position is that the facts that are found in the indictment are the facts that would found and which the Prosecution attempted to prove are the facts which would found a conviction under 7(3). We tried to prove that he was the formal de jure commander. As Mr. Morrissey pointed out, we failed. The trial judgement did that analysis and concluded that he was not formally appointed as the commander of the operation. There -- and also some of the aspects relating to the operation, as we've argued, were also not proven beyond a reasonable doubt. That doesn't mean there wasn't evidence as to the operation, as to the forward command post, and we say that the test applied to those two was wrong, but in respect of the test as to his effective control, his superior status over the subordinates, the focus of the Trial Chamber was, in fact, wrong as well, as we've pled and argued in our brief and we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, what I'm suggesting to you is that the accused would have understood the references to de jure and de facto as merely routes to his assumption of command authority. The reference to de facto would not necessarily extend beyond command authority; it would be merely a suggestion that he would have assumed his command by a process of osmosis, as it were, having regard to the slow evolution of the territorial unit into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He may have done so, but let me just assist the Court by referring to some pre-trial filings by the Defence which perhaps will aid in our consideration of the point. In the pre-trial brief at paragraph 172, the Defence summarizes the Prosecution position as follows -- I'm sorry, the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at paragraph 172 summarizes our position as follows: "The Prosecution contends the accused had effective control over the troops subordinated to him for the operation, as evidenced both by his de jure authority and the cumulative effect of the facts, which establishes that he was a de facto commander who was able to exercise effective control over the troops who committed the crimes referred to in the indictment," and there was a reference to paragraphs 5, 165 to 172 and 168 of the pre-trial brief, which also addressed the subject. In its opening statement, the Prosecution carries this theme forward. At the opening the Prosecution argued that the evidence will show that during the course of Operation Neretva, the accused did, indeed, demonstrate effective command and control by issuing orders, instruction, and directives to the units, and by ensuring their implementation he planned and was instrumental in the implementation of the military operations carried out by the units which took place -- or which took part in Neretva 93 Operation. Accordingly, under international humanitarian law, the accused clearly had the responsibility of a superior enshrined in Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. Turning to the Defence filings, which I think support the position and clarify that there was no misunderstanding as to the scope of the allegations in the indictment and that they included, indeed, superior responsibility and that it was no surprise for the Defence that we are arguing this point in our appeal. If you -- if we start at the 92 bis application dated 2 February 2004, the Defence in opposition to the Prosecution application under this article -- this rule, the Defence repeatedly refers to the evidence of the proposed 92 bis witness as going to, and I quote: "Establish that he was a superior to those who allegedly did commit the crimes." In its Defence pre-trial brief filed on the 22nd of March, 2003, the Defence argued, and I quote: "This means that the accused had neither de facto or de jure command authority or control over the units and commands taking part in the operation, nor was he in a relationship of superiority." And if you look at the Defence pre-trial brief at paragraphs 163, 164, 169, 199, and 200 you find other references to superior relationship and authority. There's a Defence addendum to the 93 [sic] bis motion of the Prosecution dated 23 August 2004. The Defence objected to Witness 4. The Defence notes: "It is the Prosecution case that Mr. Halilovic was the superior of those units of the 1st Corps sent to Herzegovina." In the final trial brief 25 August 2005, paragraph 353: "The Prosecution may not be said to have established a chain of command between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Alispago nor any evidence of effective control from the former over the latter." Also at paragraph 475: "If he was in a position of superior authority, he had to initiate an investigation, which he did." Paragraph 495: "There is no evidence whatsoever, even if one accepts the Prosecution case for the sake of argument that Mr. Halilovic was the superior of the Independent Prozor Battalion for the purpose of the operation that he could be said to be their superior as understood by Article 7(3) of the Statute." In paragraph 605: "As such, he was not in a superior/subordinate relationship vis-a-vis those troops and had no obligation under international law to punish." The accused has the right to know the case he must meet in order to properly defend himself. In practice, this means that an accused cannot be held criminally responsible, whether at trial or on appeal based on material facts not pleaded in the indictment or otherwise notified to the Defence in a clear, consistent, and timely manner. Command of the operation was alleged, but command was not indispensable for a conviction. In this case the right to a fair trial has been respected. The Prosecution pleaded material facts in the indictment to show the superior/subordinate relationship between the accused and the perpetrators of the crimes in Grabovica. It pleaded a case of effective control beyond command. Let me now turn to a discussion about the reason to know. Mr. Guenael Mettraux in his submissions postulated a legal test for when a superior is obliged to take action to prevent, and it really involves the question of when is a superior on notice of the risk of future criminal conduct, such as to put him or to crystallise the duty to act to prevent the crimes. The Prosecution's position is that the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber's formulation of the risk threshold is correct. They say it is a real and reasonable or real and reasonably foreseeable risk of crimes which triggers the superior's duty to take steps. Our submission is that the risk need not be as high as substantial likelihood, as put forward by Mr. Mettraux, which has been the risk standard adopted for 7(1) modes of liability. We say that a different threshold is justified by the special nature of superior responsibility, that the position held by a superior and the unique degree of control that a superior exercises over the actions of the perpetrator makes it appropriate for a superior to act in the face of any real or reasonably foreseeable risk. And this standard is consistent with Appeals Chamber case law on superior responsibility as -- including the Bagilishema and Celebici appeals. I refer you to Celebici at 238 and Bagilishema at paragraph 28. I also refer you to the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber decision at 155, 160, 169, 170, and 178. The reason we say that the superior should be held to this standard is that requiring proof that a superior had notice of a certainty or a near certainty of future crimes would significantly undermine the superior responsibility doctrine. It would permit a superior to sit back, do nothing, and wait until an obviously risky situation escalates into an actual or imminent commission of crimes. Requiring a superior to act in the face of a real and reasonable risk puts the onus on a superior to intervene early, in order to supervise and to take the reasonable and necessary measures to control and prevent crime. The superiors have a responsibility of enforcing the law of armed conflict as the prevention of wartime atrocities depends on the conscientious supervision of subordinates. It is our submission that to require such a high standard as put forward by counsel for Mr. Halilovic would be inappropriate. Superiors must be required to prevent the realisation of a real and reasonable risk of crimes. In terms of the case itself, I just want to highlight the background of the 9th Brigade and the knowledge that Mr. Halilovic had of its criminal behaviour. It's found in the briefs, it's found in the judgement, and I just want to highlight one fact. July 2nd and 3rd, 1993, and there's much talk of this in the judgement, there was a blockade by the 9th and 10th Brigades of several government buildings, including the ABiH operations centre in Sarajevo. The two brigades or members of them detained soldiers at gunpoint for several days, stripping them and humiliating them. The dangerous conduct of these people was known to Sefer Halilovic, because during the course of the blockade Delic -- led by Delalic and the commander of the 10th, Halilovic was contacted -- or was contacted and requested to contact Delalic to inform him -- or, I'm sorry. Halilovic contacted Delalic to inform him that the Lasva unit was planning to attack them. So he gave him advance notice of the fact that there was a possibility of a military police action against their mutiny that was pending, and that's found in trial judgement 137. Moving now to the suggestion that -- excuse me. Excuse me, I've just lost a piece of paper. Excuse me. Moving now to the examples to -- of failure to follow orders as evidence of effective control, Mr. Morrissey during the course of his response suggested that there was a different interpretation that could be given to each of these instances, suggesting that the Trial Chamber was correct in its rejection or disregard of these facts as -- the facts of the -- that the orders were followed was muted, I guess is a better way to put it, by the Trial Chamber, and having regard to the fact that there were either delays in their implementation or there were intervening discussions with Delic in the -- in the course of their implementation. The point that I was making during my submissions yesterday was not that there wasn't intervention or discussion or delay, but the point that I was making was that there was, in fact, in each of these cases a following-up and a following through of the order. Karavelic sent his troops to the operation. He accepted their subordination. Delalic was wanting to leave; Halilovic stopped him. Gusic delayed battle, and after a direction by Delic on Halilovic's insistence, he went into battle and there was an -- a report back to Halilovic about going back to -- about going into battle. Alispago, yes, tore up the order but ultimately he issued exactly the same order and carried it out. So the point was not that there was delay, that there was consultation, that there was discussion; the point was that these orders were followed. Finally, I want to comment on Mr. Mettraux's discussion and Mr. Morrissey alluded to this as well. Ex post facto and the Delic order. We do not rely on the 12th September order as the basis for the material ability to prevent and punish. If it was, I would agree with Mr. Mettraux that it would be ex post facto, but we rely on the order as confirmation of the effective control that Sefer Halilovic had over the troops, the 9th Brigade troops in particular, at the material time. More important, we rely on the order as listing all of the -- all of the reasonable measures and necessary measures that he could have taken to punish the troops. So we don't rely on it for its purpose of establishing that Mr. Halilovic was, in fact, commander on the 12th because we say that the order, in fact, confirms that he was the commander or superior of the troops prior to that date. Our position is and the evidence shows that he was superior of these troops from about the 8th when his order was accepted, and perhaps earlier from the point when his order was issued. To conclude, our submission is that there isn't anything in the response of the Defence that takes away from the submissions of the Prosecution, and I reconfirm my concluding remarks asking this Court to, with respect, accept our submissions, reverse the acquittal, and decide the case on the basis of a review of the facts and determine that Mr. Halilovic was, in fact, guilty as charged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kremer. Thank you for being brief, because you did not use up all the time that had been given to you. This being said, I am now turning to Mr. Halilovic and invite him to take the floor if he so wishes- he doesn't have to- for a brief statement of no more than ten minutes. You have the floor, Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, it is with pleasure that I wish to state that I am quite content with the hearing yesterday and today. I wish to also state that I think that the proceedings were quite fair. I do recognise that the tasks that you are discharging are quite exigent and difficult. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. If my fellow Judges and the parties have no questions or comments to make, it seems to be the case, I now will bring these proceedings to an end. The decision will be issued as early as possible. On behalf of the Appeals Chamber, I thank the counsel for Mr. Halilovic and I thank the Prosecution for their cooperation. I also thank the Legal Officers of the Appeals Chamber and the registry for their valuable cooperation throughout the proceedings, not to forget those working behind the scene for us, I mean the technicians, the court reporters, and the interpreters. I thank them for their useful cooperation. The meeting stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.56 p.m.
